name: NVIDIA L40S (AD102, compute capability 8.9)
notes: Published figures, not a measurement: no device run has confirmed any of them, and none has run here. launch_ns, link_ns, memory_efficiency, occupancy_to_saturate and memory_latency_ns are assumptions, the same on every packaged card, marked as such below.

documents.whitepaper: NVIDIA Ada GPU Architecture whitepaper, Appendix C, the L40 column (https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/geforce/ada/nvidia-ada-gpu-architecture.pdf)
documents.sections: CUDA C++ Programming Guide 12.9, section 20, Compute Capabilities, and Table 7 of arithmetic throughput (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.9.1/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html)
documents.guide: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2, Compute Capabilities, Tables 30 and 31 (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html)

source.sms: Derived: the product page gives 18,176 CUDA cores, 568 tensor cores and 142 RT cores, and an Ada SM has 128 CUDA cores, 4 tensor cores and one RT core (Ada whitepaper), so 142 SMs, as the whitepaper lists for the L40 with the same cores.
source.ghz: Derived: NVIDIA publishes no L40S clock; the product page's FP32 91.6 TFLOPS on 18,176 cores at 2 operations per fused multiply-add is 2.52 GHz.
source.dram_gbps: Product page: 48 GB GDDR6 at 864 GB/s.
source.flops: Product page: FP32 91.6 TFLOPS. i32 and f64 are derived from the Programming Guide 12.9, section 20.7.1: an 8.9 SM has 128 FP32 cores, 64 INT32 cores and 2 FP64 cores, so i32 is half of f32 and f64 1/64 of it.
source.tensor: Product page, dense (the sparse figures are twice these): TF32 183, BFLOAT16 and FP16 362.05, FP8 733 TFLOPS. The page does not name the accumulator; the model reads tensor_f16 for an f32 accumulator, as the page's figure. The others are recorded for a reader.
source.link_gbps: Product page: PCIe Gen4 x16, 64 GB/s bidirectional, so 32 GB/s each way, before protocol overhead.
source.occupancy: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2, Compute Capabilities, Tables 30 and 31 (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html), 8.9 column: an SM holds 64 K registers, 48 warps (1536 threads), 24 blocks and 100 KB of shared memory, and a block at most 1024 threads, 64 K registers, 255 registers a thread and 99 KB of shared memory, past 48 KB only by opting in. The CUDA C++ Programming Guide 12.9, section 20, says for each of 8.x, 9.0, 10.x and 12.0 that the 1 KB of shared memory not made available to a thread block is reserved for system use (shared_reserved). CUDA 13.2's occupancy calculator, cuda_occupancy.h, allocates registers a warp at a time in units of 256 (register_unit) from each of the 4 parts of the register file (partitions) and shared memory in units of 128 bytes (shared_unit), and gives compute capability 8.9 the same 24 blocks an SM; tools/checks/occupancy.py holds the card's resident blocks to that calculator (evidence/v1_2/occupancy).
source.shared_bytes_per_clock: CUDA C++ Programming Guide: shared memory has 32 banks, each 32 bits wide a clock cycle.
source.memory_latency_ns: Assumed. NVIDIA publishes no device-memory latency and no run here has measured one; it prices only a pipeline's asynchronous copies, as the bytes in flight over this latency. Every packaged card assumes the same 500 ns.
